title: ISO/IEC 42001 and the Microsoft Responsible AI Standard
summary: ISO/IEC 42001 is a certifiable management system standard for how an organization governs AI. Microsoft's Responsible AI Standard is an internal rulebook that Microsoft released externally. Neither certifies one chatbot.
useIf: A customer asks for a certificate, or you are designing an internal AI governance rulebook.
avoidIf: You want to certify a single application's behaviour or prove EU AI Act compliance with a certificate alone.

explain.md: **ISO/IEC 42001:2023** is a management system standard for artificial intelligence, an **AIMS**, published in December 2023. It follows Plan-Do-Check-Act and governs an organization's AI practice, not one application's behaviour. It is certifiable: an external audit assesses whether your management system meets the standard [[r12]]. As with other ISO management system standards, expect elements such as a policy, defined roles, risk assessment, operational controls, monitoring, internal audit, management review and improvement (general pattern, not clause by clause).

The **Microsoft Responsible AI Standard v2** (June 2022) is an internal standard that Microsoft released externally. It has six goal groups: Accountability, Transparency, Fairness, Reliability and Safety, Privacy and Security, and Inclusiveness. Accountability includes goal A5, human oversight and control, and a **Sensitive Uses review** that is repeated at least annually (A2.3) [[r13]]. It is a rulebook for one company's engineering teams, not a certification you can obtain.

explain.title: How the two fit together
explain.md: Use ISO/IEC 42001 as the outer assurance wrapper that an auditor can inspect, and a rulebook like the Responsible AI Standard as a model for the inner checkpoints that product teams pass before launch and at each review. One answers 'can you show a working system of management', the other answers 'what must this team do before it ships'.

explain.title: The Plan-Do-Check-Act loop of an AIMS
explain.alt: Plan covers scope, policy and risk assessment, Do covers controls and operation, Check covers monitoring and audit, Act covers corrective action, and the loop returns to Plan.
explain.src:
flowchart LR
  P[Plan scope policy risk] --> D[Do controls and operation]
  D --> C[Check monitor and audit]
  C --> A[Act correct and improve]
  A --> P

pitfalls.symptom: Marketing says the chatbot is ISO 42001 certified
pitfalls.cause: Certification of the organization's management system was read as product certification
pitfalls.fix: Say 'our AI management system is certified' and state the scope; never imply a model or app is certified

pitfalls.symptom: A certificate exists but nobody follows the process
pitfalls.cause: The AIMS is a paper exercise without operating evidence
pitfalls.fix: Run internal audits, track corrective actions and keep records for each control

pitfalls.symptom: A rulebook is ignored by product teams
pitfalls.cause: Goals were not translated into reviews and release gates
pitfalls.fix: Turn goals into checkpoints, for example a Sensitive Uses review before launch and annually after

scenarios.title: An RFP requires an AI management certificate
scenarios.situation: A large buyer's RFP requires evidence of an AI management system, ideally a certificate. The supplier has solid engineering practices but no formal system.
constraints: A multi-year contract depends on it
unknowns: What scope should the AIMS cover?
scenarios.question: What do you do?

options.name: Scope an AIMS under ISO/IEC 42001, close gaps, run internal audits and seek certification
options.why: The buyer wants third-party assurance, and a certifiable standard is built for that.
options.tradeoff: Audit cost, process overhead and ongoing surveillance.

options.name: Send the internal rulebook and a NIST mapping
options.tradeoff: Self-assessed, so it may not satisfy a certificate requirement.

options.name: Claim the product is certified once the organization is
options.why: The certificate covers the management system, not the product's behaviour.

flips.then: A NIST mapping plus evidence pack may do.

flips.if: The scope is a single product line
flips.then: Define the AIMS scope narrowly and say so.

scenarios.takeaway: Certificates assure the system of management, not the chatbot.

scenarios.title: First internal governance programme
scenarios.situation: A mid-size company with several AI features wants consistent rules but has no external certification driver.
scenarios.question: What do you set up first?

options.name: An internal rulebook with goals like accountability and human oversight, plus a Sensitive Uses review at launch and annually
options.why: It creates enforceable checkpoints without audit cost, and follows a published model.
options.tradeoff: Self-assessed, so credibility with buyers is limited.

options.name: Leave each team to decide
options.why: Inconsistent controls and no accountable owner.

flips.then: Convert the rulebook into an AIMS.

scenarios.takeaway: Start with enforceable checkpoints. Add assurance when it pays.

quiz.q: What does an ISO/IEC 42001 certificate attest?
options: A specific chatbot is safe and legal
The organization's AI management system meets the standard
The organization complies with the EU AI Act
quiz.explain: 42001 is a management system standard. It governs the organization's AI practice, not one application's behaviour, and it is not an EU AI Act compliance certificate [[r12]].

quiz.q: How many goal groups does the Microsoft Responsible AI Standard v2 define?
quiz.explain: Accountability, Transparency, Fairness, Reliability and Safety, Privacy and Security, and Inclusiveness [[r13]].

quiz.q: No customer or regulator requires certification. Which first step fits best?
options: An ISO audit within a month
An internal rulebook with launch and annual reviews
quiz.explain: A rulebook creates checkpoints cheaply. An immediate audit is heavy without existing processes, and waiting for an incident is reactive.

flashcards.back: A certifiable AI management system standard (AIMS), published December 2023, run as Plan-Do-Check-Act. It governs organizational practice, not one application's behaviour.

flashcards.front: What are the six goal groups of Microsoft's RAI Standard v2?
flashcards.back: Accountability, Transparency, Fairness, Reliability and Safety, Privacy and Security, Inclusiveness. Includes A5 human oversight and an annual Sensitive Uses review.
EU AI Act is law. NIST is voluntary guidance. ISO 42001 is a certifiable standard. The RAI Standard is an internal rulebook.
